t: Count Caesar Cipher Pairs — Rotation-Invariant Keys
o: Applying the cyclic shift to one string changes every letter by the same offset, so two strings are similar iff one is a rotation of the other's alphabet values. Normalize each word by subtracting its first letter mod 26: the resulting difference tuple is invariant under Caesar shifts, so similar words share identical keys. Count pairs per key with c·(c−1)/2. Example: 'fusion' and 'layout' share the normalized pattern (0,15,18,8,14,13) after shifting.
k: Normalize by (ch − ch₀) mod 26 relative to the first character — shift-invariant canonical form.
Pairs per equivalence class of size c contribute c(c−1)/2.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Map of Normalized Keys
a.i: Map each word to its difference tuple, count class sizes, and sum combinations.
s: For each word compute key = tuple((ord(c) − ord(w[0])) mod 26).
Count occurrences per key in a hash map.
a.t: O(total characters) = O(n·m) hashing work, within the n·m ≤ 1e5 bound

a.i: For each pair, test similarity directly by checking whether words[i] shifted by some offset equals words[j] — comparing differences relative to the first characters. O(n²·m), acceptable only for tiny inputs.
s: For each pair (i, j), compute d = (ords of j minus ords of i) mod 26 relative to first chars.
Similar iff all differences equal d.

w: The normalization trick is the whole problem — recognize that 'apply shifts to either string any number of times' means similarity is an equivalence relation under rotation. Pitfalls: negative mod results in C++/Java/JS (add 26), and pair counts overflowing 32 bits when n = 1e5 identical words (use 64-bit before casting). Follow-up: allow shifts by different amounts per position (then keys become full difference vectors), or count triples.
